reason: Both pages get the main finding across with correct numbers: 9 of 11 at 0 of 29, Wilson 0-12% (about 1 in 8), 23% chance of a clean run at a 1-in-20 rate, and 73/381 clean tries. B is the more engaging piece. Its step 4 asks the reader to guess before the 20 simulated tests run, and 'Run 20 more tests' builds up a running tally (20 of 80 clean). Its step 5 per-model interval chart with '9 models, same score, same range' makes the point that the test cannot rank models. A won because it is more complete and more honest for a public post. Step 3 shows three real trap requests, and step 4's grid of 319 replies by category adds the 23 ordinary questions so the clean scores are not read as blanket refusal. The takeaway names the other limits: one reply per request, rules spelled out in the prompt, no breaks on the 13 write/file requests (ceiling), and the 'refused' label that cannot be trusted. B ends with only the tries-needed chart, and in steps 4 and 6 it reuses its 'Refused, or did only the allowed part' colour for simulated runs and tries bars. A's always-visible luck slider is accurate (1% gives 75%, 10% gives 4.7%) but sits outside the card and does not change the scenes.

A: The 'Try it' luck slider sits under every scene, disconnected from the card; moving it does not change the simulation or curve shown above, so it reads as a separate widget.
Fine print at phone width is very small (takeaway footnote, heatmap column headers, view 5 run labels) and hard to read on a LinkedIn phone feed.
It plays as a 60 s timeline that starts automatically; the last scene holds from 60 s and the earlier scenes go by fast unless the reader pauses or scrubs.
B: The legend's blue 'Refused, or did only the allowed part' is reused for the simulated model's clean dots (step 4) and for the tries-needed bars (step 6), where that meaning does not apply.
It leaves out the test's other limits: one reply per request, rules spelled out in the prompt, the ceiling on the 13 write/file requests, and the 23 ordinary questions answered correctly.
Legend items not used in a step are dimmed to very low contrast (steps 1, 2, 6), and the handwritten display font is softer to read on the small step titles and annotations.
